opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When we started SGLang, the motivation came from what we were seeing in how people actually used large language models. It was no longer just a single prompt and a single answer. People were building more complex programs: multi-turn chat, agents calling tools, few-shot prompting, chain-of-thought, running many parallel samples and then picking the best one, asking the model to output structured formats like JSON. These workloads have a lot of structure, but the serving systems at the time mostly treated each request as an isolated piece of text.

So we wanted to do two things at once. On the front end, we wanted to give developers a simple, flexible way to express these LLM programs, with control flow, parallelism, and constrained outputs, without hand-writing messy glue code. On the back end, we wanted a runtime that could take advantage of that structure to be much faster. A good example is RadixAttention. Many of these calls share long common prefixes, like the same system prompt, the same few-shot examples, or the same conversation history. Instead of recomputing that every time, we keep the KV cache in a radix tree and reuse it automatically across requests. We also worked on things like fast constrained decoding for structured outputs and efficient scheduling.

The bigger hope was to make serving LLMs efficient and accessible to everyone, not just a few companies with huge infrastructure teams. We wanted an open-source system that researchers and companies could use, extend, and run in production at low cost. Seeing the community grow around it, with people deploying it at real scale and contributing back, has honestly gone beyond what we imagined at the beginning.

r001.rationale: The response describes combining a developer-facing programming interface with a serving runtime, but does not say SGLang unified separate strands of Ying Sheng’s prior LLM inference research.

r002.rationale: It says the goal was an open-source serving system that people could run in production, alongside a runtime designed to make serving faster.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When we started SGLang, the honest answer is that we were frustrated. This was back in 2023, and we were building applications on top of large language models at Berkeley, things like agents, multi-step reasoning, and structured outputs. And every time we wanted to do something a little more complex than a single prompt-and-response, the tooling fell apart. You'd write a bunch of glue code, make many separate calls, and the inference backend treated every call as if it were independent, even when ninety percent of the prompt was identical to the one you'd just sent.

So the original goal had two sides. On the frontend, I wanted a way to express these complex programs naturally, where you could write a generation call, branch, loop, enforce a JSON schema, and have it feel like ordinary programming rather than string manipulation. On the backend, I wanted the runtime to actually understand that structure and exploit it. The key insight became RadixAttention, which is essentially automatic prefix caching organized as a radix tree. If you share a system prompt or a few-shot example across thousands of requests, you should compute it once, not every time.

What I hoped for, really, was to close the gap between how people wanted to use these models and how the serving systems were built. The models were getting more capable, but the infrastructure was still designed for chatbots. I wanted it to be designed for programs.

I did not expect it to grow the way it has. At the beginning I thought of it as a research project, something to publish and maybe maintain for a while. The fact that companies now run it in production serving enormous traffic, and that it became a community with hundreds of contributors, was not the plan. But it does validate the original intuition: performance and programmability are not opposing goals. If you design for both from the start, you get something people actually want to use.

r002.rationale: The response says he initially viewed SGLang as a research project and did not expect production adoption; it does not state production readiness was an initial goal.

astra-6.text: The goal was to make it easier to build and run applications with large language models efficiently. When you build an application, you often need more than a single model call—you might have multiple calls, branching logic, and intermediate results that can be reused. We wanted SGLang to make those workflows easier to express and give the runtime enough information to execute them efficiently. So the idea was to bring programmability and performance together, rather than making developers handle all the optimization themselves.

sol-6.1.text: When we started SGLang, we wanted to make it easier to build applications with language models and run them efficiently. A lot of applications involve more than a single prompt—you might have multiple model calls, branching, or shared context. We wanted a programming interface that could express those workflows naturally, together with a runtime that could optimize their execution. The idea was to make the application easier to write while also making inference faster and more cost-effective.
